'''''Khaya senegalensis''''' is a species of tree in the [[Meliaceae]] family that is native to [[Africa]]. Common names include African mahogany, dry zone mahogany, Gambia mahogany, khaya wood, Senegal mahogany, cailcedra, ''acajou'', ''djalla'', and ''bois rouge''.

==Description==
[[File:Khaya_senegalensis_Fanling_Station.jpg|thumb|left|Mature tree next to [[Fanling Station]] (Hong Kong)]]
African mahogany is a fast-growing medium-sized tree which can obtain a height of up to {{convert|15|-|30|m|abbr=on}} in height and {{convert|1|m|abbr=on}} in diameter. The bark is dark grey to grey-brown while the heartwood is brown with a pink-red pigment made up of coarse interlocking grains. The tree is characterised by leaves arranged in a spiral formation clustered at the end of branches. The white flowers are sweet-scented; the fruit changes from grey to black when ripening.

==Distribution and habitat==
The tree is native to [[Benin]], [[Burkina Faso]], [[Cameroon]], [[Central African Republic]], [[Chad]], [[Ivory Coast]], [[Gabon]], [[Gambia]], [[Ghana]], [[Guinea]], [[Guinea-Bissau]], [[Mali]], [[Niger]], [[Nigeria]],  [[Senegal]], [[Sierra Leone]], [[Sudan]], [[Togo]], and [[Uganda]]. It is found in [[Riparian forest|riparian forests]] and higher-rainfall savannah woodlands; in moist regions, it is found on higher ground. Within its first year, the seedling develops a deep root system that makes it the most drought resistant member of its genus.

==Uses==
''K. senegalensis'' has been extensively studied for [[trypanocidal]] activity. Atawodi et al 2003, Wurochekke and Nok 2004, Mikail 2009, Aderbauer et al 2008, Umar et al 2010, Adeiza et al 2010, Ibrahim et al 2008, and Ibrahim et al 2013a investigate [[extract]]s of [[stem bark]] both ''in vitro'' and ''in vivo'' in rats, against ''[[Trypanosoma evansi|T. evansi]]'', ''[[Trypanosoma congolense|T. congolense]]'' and ''[[Trypanosoma brucei brucei|T. b. brucei]]''. All showed promising results and a few demonstrated an effective dose.<ref name="Ibrahim-et-al-2014">{{cite journal | last1=Ibrahim | first1=Mohammed Auwal | last2=Mohammed | first2=Aminu | last3=Isah | first3=Murtala Bindawa | last4=Aliyu | first4=Abubakar Babando | title=Anti-trypanosomal activity of African medicinal plants: A review update | journal=[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]] | publisher=[[International Society of Ethnopharmacology]] (ISE) | volume=154 | issue=1 | year=2014 | issn=0378-8741 | doi=10.1016/j.jep.2014.04.012 | pages=26–54}}</ref>

The wood is used for a variety of purposes, including carpentry (e.g., interior trim) and construction. Traditionally, the wood was used for [[Dugout (boat)|dugout canoes]], household implements, [[djembe]], and fuel.

The bitter tasting bark is used for a variety of medical purposes; it is taken against fever caused by malaria, stomach ailments, and headaches. Applied externally, it is used to treat skin rashes, wounds, and abnormalities.

Ethnobotanical and ethnopharmacological literature has reported use of ''Khaya senegalensis'' stem bark in women's reproductive health contexts, including for irregular menstruation.<ref name="Njamen2013">{{cite journal |last=Njamen |first=D. |display-authors=etal |title=Phytotherapy and Women's Reproductive Health |journal=Planta Medica |year=2013 |doi=10.1055/s-0032-1328326 |pmid=23539352 }}</ref> A 2025 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (''n''=84) evaluated ''K. senegalensis'' in women experiencing menstrual pain and reported reductions in daily pain ratings and menstrual distress over one menstrual cycle.<ref name="Lopresti2025">{{cite journal |last=Lopresti |first=A. L. |display-authors=etal |title=An Examination into the Safety and Efficacy of a ''Khaya senegalensis'' Preparation on Women Experiencing Menstrual Pain and Menstrual Distress: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial |journal=International Journal of Women's Health |year=2025 |volume=17 |pages=2025–2038 |doi=10.2147/IJWH.S521349 |doi-access=free |pmid=40672875 |pmc=12266064}}</ref>

It has been exported from West Africa (Gambia) to Europe since the first half of the 19th century and has been exploited heavily for its timber. It is now used more locally, and is planted ornamentally to line roads.

==Conservation and threats==
''K. senegalensis'' has experienced high amounts of exploitation, and little regeneration takes place once disturbance occurs. Because of this, the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species considers it a vulnerable species. The only conservation which takes place are log export bans and legal protection in some countries.[[File:Khaya senegalensis MHNT.BOT.2004.0.225 Fruit.jpg|thumb|''Khaya senegalensis'' - [[MHNT]]]]
